issues.legal_issue: Delay and laches do not bar constitutional relief when the State has continuously deprived a person of property without lawful authority and the circumstances make refusal of relief unjust.
material_facts: The authorities took possession of the land without completing acquisition proceedings and transferred it for public development.
The owners repeatedly sought compensation and pursued the authorities; a later attempt to acquire the land also lapsed.
The owners were illiterate and inarticulate, and the State conceded their ownership.
The High Court rejected their claim on delay and missing-record grounds, although no third-party interest was identified.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in refusing relief on the grounds of delay and missing records; the claim was not barred by delay and laches.
issues.legal_principle: The discretion to refuse relief under Article 226 for delay must be exercised fairly and on the facts; delay is not an absolute bar where the cause of action continues, the claim is legally sustainable, and substantial justice requires relief. The Court relied on P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of T.N., State of M.P. v. Nandlal Jaiswal, Tridip Kumar Dingal v. State of West Bengal, Durga Prasad v. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Co. v. District Board, Dayal Singh v. Union of India, Shankara Co-op Housing Society v. M. Prabhakar, and H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_claim and state_possession_without_law and continuing_claim_efforts and no_third_party_interest

predicates.constitutional_writ_claim: The claimant seeks constitutional-court relief concerning the State's treatment of property.
predicates.state_possession_without_law: State authorities took possession of a person's property without completing a legally authorized process.
predicates.continuing_claim_efforts: The affected person continued to seek relief from the authorities after the property was taken.
predicates.no_third_party_interest: No third party acquired an interest that would be harmed by granting relief.

issues.definition: When a constitutional property claim follows State possession without lawful process, the claimant continued pursuing relief, and no third-party interest would be harmed, delay does not bar relief.

issues.legal_issue: The State may not take or retain a person's property without authority of law and must use a legally prescribed process to acquire it.
material_facts: The owners' predecessors held title to the land, and the State authorities took physical possession in 1964.
The initial acquisition proceedings lapsed, and a later acquisition attempt also lapsed without completion.
The State did not claim title and conceded the owners' right, title, and interest in the land.
The authorities nevertheless retained and transferred possession without completing acquisition or paying compensation.
issues.conclusion: The State's possession without a lawful acquisition process was impermissible, and the owners were entitled to lawful acquisition and compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300-A permits deprivation of property only by authority of law and through a procedure prescribed by statute; executive action alone cannot deprive a person of property. The Court relied on Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat. It also recognized the right to property as a human right, relying on Lachhman Dass v. Jagat Ram, Amarjit Singh v. State of Punjab, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar, and Delhi Airtech Services v. State of U.P.

predicates.property_deprivation_claim: A person seeks relief because the State has taken or retained that person's property.
predicates.state_possession_without_law: State authorities took possession without completing a legally authorized process.
predicates.owner_title_conceded: The State accepted that the affected person held title to the property.

issues.definition: When the State has taken property without lawful process and accepts the claimant's title, it must use a lawful acquisition process.

issues.legal_issue: Depriving a person of property that supports the person's livelihood engages the right to life and requires adequate compensation and rehabilitation.
material_facts: The owners were farmers whose land was taken without compensation or replacement land.
They had no other vocation or business to rely on for their livelihood.
The authorities did not provide compensation or rehabilitation despite the owners' efforts.
issues.conclusion: The deprivation violated Article 21, and the State had a legal obligation to provide adequate compensation and rehabilitate the persons uprooted by its actions.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 protects the right to life, which the Court applied to the circumstances of persons deprived of property on which their livelihood depended. In a welfare State, statutory authorities must provide adequate compensation and rehabilitate persons uprooted by State action. The Court also relied on K. Krishna Reddy v. Special Deputy Collector, Land Acquisition, which emphasized that compensation should be determined without delay because its value and utility diminish over time.

predicates.property_deprivation_claim: A person claims that the State deprived that person of property.
predicates.livelihood_depends_on_property: The affected person's livelihood depends on the property taken.
predicates.state_caused_displacement: The State's taking of the property uprooted the affected person without providing a substitute means of support.

issues.definition: When the State's taking of property on which a person's livelihood depends uproots that person, the State must compensate and rehabilitate that person.

issues.legal_issue: When the State offers to complete acquisition of land it has taken without completing the earlier process, the acquisition must be completed and compensation paid under the applicable statutory process.
material_facts: The State offered to issue a fresh acquisition notification, complete the subsequent statutory steps, make an award, and pay compensation with statutory benefits.
The Court accepted the State's proposal to resolve the owners' claim.
The owners were to retain the right to pursue statutory remedies for enhanced compensation.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the authorities to complete acquisition expeditiously, assess market value as of publication of the acquisition notification, pay the award and statutory benefits, and preserve the owners' right to seek enhancement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its provisions for notification, declaration, notice, award, and compensation under Sections 4, 6, and 9, and relied on the State's undertaking to complete the process. It directed that market value be assessed as of publication of the Section 4 notification and that statutory benefits be paid.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The matter is an appeal challenging a decision that refused constitutional relief.
predicates.state_offers_to_complete_acquisition: The State proposes to complete the statutory process for acquiring the property.
predicates.prior_state_possession: State authorities had already taken possession of the property before completing acquisition.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the refusal of constitutional relief, the State offers to complete acquisition, and it already holds possession, the State must complete acquisition and pay compensation.
